what_it_does: Modern chips (SoCs — system-on-chips) pack a CPU, a GPU, and a neural-network accelerator (NPU) on the same piece of silicon, sharing the same main memory. To prevent one component from reading or tampering with another's data, hardware can protect memory using a message authentication code (MAC) — a short cryptographic fingerprint stored alongside every chunk of data — plus an integrity tree (a chain of hashes from individual data blocks up to a single trusted root) that lets the hardware detect any tampering. The problem is that the fixed chunk size baked into conventional designs works well for the predictable, fine-grained access pattern of a CPU but is a poor fit for the very large, irregular bursts that GPUs and NPUs produce, causing slowdown. This paper proposes a unified protection scheme that stores MACs and tree nodes at four different granularities and automatically selects the right granularity for each region of memory based on which processor is using it and how.
